t: The Number of Good Subsets: Bitmask DP over Small Primes
o: A subset is good when its product factors into distinct primes, i.e., the product is squarefree and greater than 1. In [1,2,3,4] the value 4 = 2*2 can never join a good subset, while the lone 1 doubles every option: the meaningful picks are {2}, {3}, and {2,3}, giving 3 * 2 = 6 subsets in total. In [4,2,3,15] the value 15 = 3*5 is usable but clashes with 3 since together they repeat the prime 3, leaving exactly [2], [3], [15], [2,3], [2,15] for an answer of five. Because nums[i] is at most 30, only ten primes ever matter (2 through 29), so every value collapses to a 10-bit mask of those primes; the up-to-100000 input elements therefore reduce to multiplicities of at most 30 distinct values.
k: A good product is exactly a squarefree product over the 10 primes up to 30, so each usable value maps to a 10-bit mask and combinations become bitwise ORs.
Any value containing a repeated prime factor (4, 8, 9, 12, ...) can never appear in a good subset and must be excluded entirely.
Each 1 doubles every good subset independently, so count subsets built from values above 1 and multiply by 2 raised to the number of 1s.
Equal values are interchangeable copies: including value v contributes cnt[v] independent ways.

a.i: Only squarefree values matter, and each maps to a mask over the 10 relevant primes; a partial selection stays valid exactly while its masks keep every prime unshared, which a running used-mask enforces naturally. Recurse over distinct values with multiplicities, branching on take or skip. Multiply the count of nonempty prime-set selections by 2^ones for the freely includable ones.
s: Count occurrences of each value and strip the 1s into their own counter.
Convert each distinct value to its prime mask, discarding values with any repeated prime factor.
Recurse take/skip per distinct value, taking value v only when its mask is disjoint from the used mask, multiplying by its count.
At the leaf return 1 if at least one prime was used, else 0.
a.t: Roughly O(2^d) where d is the number of distinct squarefree values in [2,30] (at most 18), so about 262144 leaf paths; counting the input adds O(n).
a.sp: O(d) recursion depth plus constant-size tables.

a.n: Approach 2: Knapsack DP over Prime Masks
a.i: Think knapsack over masks: dp[mask] counts selections of values whose combined prime set is exactly mask. Processing each distinct squarefree value v with multiplicity c transitions dp[s | m_v] += dp[s] * c whenever s and m_v are disjoint, iterating s downward so each batch of equal values is consumed once. The answer is (sum over all masks minus the empty selection) scaled by 2^ones.
s: Count occurrences of every value from 2 to 30 and tally how many 1s exist.
For each present value compute its prime mask; skip it if any prime exponent exceeds one.
Initialize dp[0] = 1; iterate masks s from high to low, and when s and m_v are disjoint add dp[s] * cnt[v] to dp[s | m_v].
Sum dp[mask] over all nonzero masks and subtract the empty selection counted in dp[0].
Multiply by fast-power 2^ones modulo 10^9 + 7 and return.
a.t: O(n + 30 * 2^10) since counting is linear and the knapsack relaxes about 1024 masks for each of up to 30 candidate values (with fast exponentiation for the final scaling).
a.sp: O(2^10) for one DP entry per prime mask.

w: Present bitmask DP as your main solution and fall back to backtracking only if the knapsack view does not click. Classic mistakes: letting squared-prime values like 4, 8, 9 or 12 slip in, forgetting to subtract the empty selection before scaling, misapplying the modulus to negative intermediates, and overlooking that every 1 doubles the count. Follow-ups worth mentioning: raise the value bound (more primes, wider masks) or reconstruct the actual subsets instead of counting them.
